title: Lemma 20.8.13
text: Lemma 20.8.13 . DA69AEE4E88A Let $\mu :Y\to X$ be a modification and let $F$ be an effective $\mu $-exceptional real divisor. For a big class $\alpha $, \[  \operatorname {Vol}(\mu ^*\alpha +t\{ F\} )=\operatorname {Vol}(\alpha ) \quad (t\geq 0), \qquad \langle (\mu ^*\alpha )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ F\} =0.  \] Proof. Pulling back a positive current in $\alpha $ and adding $t[F]$ proves the inequality $\geq $: the absolutely continuous top mass is unchanged over the common isomorphism locus. Conversely, pushing forward any positive current in $\mu ^*\alpha +t\{ F\} $ gives a positive current in $\alpha $, with the same absolutely continuous top mass on that locus. The exceptional analytic sets have Lebesgue measure zero, so the reverse inequality follows from the defining supremum of volume. This also proves birational invariance of volume when $t=0$. The derivative formula in theorem 10.99.8 on the big cone, applied on $Y$, identifies the right derivative at $t=0$ with $n\langle (\mu ^*\alpha )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ F\} $. The displayed constant-volume identity makes that derivative zero. $\square$

title: Lemma 20.8.14
text: Lemma 20.8.14 . B50F0B700160 For a big class $\beta $ and its divisorial negative part $N(\beta )$, \[  \langle \beta ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ N(\beta )\} =0.  \] Proof. Let $T_{\min }\in \beta $ have minimal singularities. Its generic divisor coefficients are those of $N(\beta )$, so Siu decomposition gives $T_{\min }-s[N(\beta )]\geq 0$ for $0\leq s\leq 1$. Only finitely many divisors occur: their support is contained in that of any gently analytic Kähler current in the big class. Removing their integration currents does not change the non-pluripolar top mass, because the currents agree off those divisors and all the products give the divisors zero mass. The maximal-mass characterization of volume thus gives \[  \operatorname {Vol}(\beta -s\{ N(\beta )\} ) \geq \int _ X\langle (T_{\min }-s[N(\beta )])^ n\rangle =\operatorname {Vol}(\beta ).  \] The reverse inequality is pseudoeffective monotonicity of volume. These classes are big since their volume is positive. Differentiate the constant-volume identity at $s=0$ using theorem 10.99.8 . The derivative is $-n\langle \beta ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ N(\beta )\} $, proving the claim. $\square$

title: Lemma 20.8.15
text: Lemma 20.8.15 . 41D346BEA9CE For a big class $\alpha $ and a prime divisor $D\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$, \[  \langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} =0.  \] Proof. For every sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, the class $\beta _\varepsilon =\alpha -\varepsilon [\omega ]$ is big. Its minimal generic Lelong number along $D$ is strictly positive. Indeed, if it were zero, Demailly's gentle analytic regularization of a current with minimal singularities in $\beta _\varepsilon $ would give a current $T_ j\in \beta _\varepsilon $ with $T_ j\geq -\frac12\varepsilon \omega $, analytic singularities, and zero generic Lelong number along $D$. A gentle approximant is smooth off its analytic pole set, and zero generic Lelong number means that this pole set does not contain $D$. Hence it is smooth near a general point of $D$, and $T_ j+\varepsilon \omega $ would be a Kähler current in $\alpha $ smooth at such a point, contrary to $D\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha )$. Thus $D$ occurs with a positive coefficient in $N(\beta _\varepsilon )$. The preceding lemma 20.8.14 gives \[  \langle \beta _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot N(\beta _\varepsilon )=0.  \] Each summand in this pairing is nonnegative: the positive-product class is a limit of pushforwards of nef powers, and its pairing with any effective divisor is nonnegative. The positive coefficient of $D$ therefore forces $\langle \beta _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} =0$. The continuous full volume-gradient formula now allows $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, proving the assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 20.8.16
search_title: Restricted equality from smooth divisor derivative
text: Proposition 20.8.16 . 7ED04B77FCC6 Let $\alpha $ be big on a compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$. For every prime divisor $D$, \[  \langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D} =\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} , \qquad \langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D}=0 \  \Longleftrightarrow \  D\subset E_{\mathrm{nK}}(\alpha ).  \] Proof. For $n=1$, work on the connected component containing the point $D$. The top real cohomology is one dimensional, and a big class has positive degree, so it is a positive multiple of a Kähler class. Its non-Kähler locus is empty, its positive product of order zero is $1$, and the zero-dimensional restricted mass of $D$ is $1$. Both assertions follow. Hence assume $n\geq 2$. First suppose $D\not\subset E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$. For each $\varepsilon >0$, regularization of a minimal current in $\alpha $ with zero generic Lelong number along $D$, followed by addition of $\varepsilon \omega $, gives a Kähler current in $\alpha _\varepsilon =\alpha +\varepsilon [\omega ]$ smooth near a general point of $D$. Thus $D$ meets its Kähler locus. Resolve $D$ by a modification $\mu :Z\to X$ which is an isomorphism near a general point of $D$, and write $\mu ^*D=\widetilde D+F$, with $F\geq 0$ exceptional and $\widetilde D$ smooth. The strict transform meets the Kähler locus of $\mu ^*\alpha _\varepsilon $. For completeness, a Kähler current smooth generically on $D$ pulls back to a current dominating $\delta \mu ^*\omega $; the standard exceptional logarithmic correction on the resolution replaces this by a Kähler lower bound, adding only exceptional poles. No pole contains $\widetilde D$. Apply theorem 20.8.3 on $Z$ and the full volume-gradient formula theorem 10.99.8 there. Birational invariance of restricted volume lemma 20.8.11 , then lemma 20.8.13 , give \[  \langle \alpha _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D} =\langle (\mu ^*\alpha _\varepsilon )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ \widetilde D\}  =\langle (\mu ^*\alpha _\varepsilon )^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \mu ^*\{ D\} .  \] Birational invariance of volume for all small perturbations in the direction $\{ D\} $ and its differentiability identify the last expression with $\langle \alpha _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} $. The defining one-sided limit for numerical restricted volume gives \[  \lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \langle \alpha _\varepsilon ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D} =\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle _{X\mid D}.  \] Indeed, if $F(s)$ is the defining supremum over positive currents with analytic singularities in $\alpha +s[\omega ]$ whose poles do not contain $D$, then $F$ is increasing and the two sides are respectively $\lim _{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\lim _{s\downarrow \varepsilon }F(s)$ and $\lim _{s\downarrow 0}F(s)$. They agree by monotonicity. Continuity of the full volume gradient proves the desired equality. If $D\subset E_{\mathrm{nn}}(\alpha )$, the numerical restricted volume is zero by definition. The coefficient of $D$ in $N(\alpha )$ is positive, so lemma 20.8.14 and the nonnegativity of the separate divisor pairings give $\langle \alpha ^{n-1}\rangle \cdot \{ D\} =0$ as well. It remains to identify the zero locus. Containment in the non-Kähler locus gives zero positive-product pairing by lemma 20.8.15 , and therefore zero restricted volume by the equality already proved. Otherwise a Kähler current $T\in \alpha $, with the permitted analytic singularities and no pole containing $D$, satisfies $T\geq \delta \omega $ for some $\delta >0$. It is an admissible competitor, and its restricted integral is at least $\delta ^{n-1}\int _ D\omega ^{n-1}>0$. This proves the converse. $\square$

title: 10.101 Balanced forms and movable classes
text: Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 2$. Write $H^{p,p}_{\mathbb R}(X)$ for real Bott–Chern cohomology, identified with the real $(p,p)$ part of de Rham cohomology. The Kähler $\partial \bar\partial $ lemma, in the form of Bott–Chern, Dolbeault and Aeppli cohomology on a compact Kähler manifold , also identifies \[  H^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}(X) \simeq H_ A^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R) =\frac{\{ T\text{ real of type }(1,1):\partial \bar\partial T=0\} }{\{ \partial \overline S+\bar\partial S:S\text{ of type }(1,0)\} }.  \] The same quotients may be formed with smooth forms or currents. These are the Kähler cohomology identifications. Let $\mathcal P_ A$ be the cone of Aeppli classes of positive $\partial \bar\partial $-closed $(1,1)$-currents, and let $\mathcal B$ be the set of classes of smooth strictly positive closed $(n-1,n-1)$-forms. The positive-matrix root formula in the proof of the Gauduchon criterion for positivity identifies these forms exactly with $\gamma ^{n-1}$ for balanced Hermitian metrics $\gamma $. Here and below all pairings are integration, with the same fixed normalization of $dd^ c$ on the two factors. Lemma 10.101.1 . 255F6B93CCE9 The cone $\mathcal P_ A$ is closed and contains no line. Under the integration pairing, \[  \mathcal B=\operatorname {Int}(\mathcal P_ A^\vee ), \qquad \overline{\mathcal B}=\mathcal P_ A^\vee .  \] Proof. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $. If $T\geq 0$, then $\int _ XT\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$ is its trace mass, is zero only for $T=0$, and depends only on the Aeppli class of $T$. Consequently, positive currents in a bounded set of Aeppli classes have bounded trace masses. Weak compactness for positive currents and continuity of pairing with smooth closed forms show that $\mathcal P_ A$ is closed. The positive mass functional also proves that it contains no line and that a positive current of zero Aeppli class is zero. If $\Gamma $ is smooth strictly positive and closed, then $\Gamma \geq \varepsilon \omega ^{n-1}$ for some $\varepsilon >0$. Thus $\int _ X\Gamma \wedge T>0$ for every nonzero positive $\partial \bar\partial $-closed current $T$. Conversely, suppose that $b\in H^{n-1,n-1}_{\mathbb R}(X)$ pairs strictly positively with every nonzero element of $\mathcal P_ A$. Choose a smooth real closed representative $\rho $ of $b$. If no representative of $b$ were strictly positive, the affine space \[  \rho +dd^ c C^\infty _{n-2,n-2}(X,\mathbb R)  \] would be disjoint from the open convex cone of smooth strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-forms. The $\partial \bar\partial $ lemma says that this affine space consists of all smooth representatives of $b$ of the given type. Hahn–Banach separation, with its sign chosen positive on the open cone, gives a nonzero continuous real linear functional $T$ such that \[  T(dd^ c\Psi )=0\quad \hbox{for every smooth real }\Psi , \qquad T(\rho )\leq 0, \qquad T(\Gamma )\geq 0\quad (\Gamma >0).  \] Indeed, the affine directions force the first equality; scaling the positive cone and then taking its closure gives the other two inequalities. This functional is a positive $(1,1)$-current and $dd^ cT=0$. Its Aeppli class is nonzero by the mass observation, contrary to the strict positivity assumption on $b$. Therefore $b\in \mathcal B$. The trace-one slice of $\mathcal P_ A$ is compact: it is the image of the weakly compact set of positive pluriharmonic currents of mass one. Strict positivity on this slice is consequently equivalent to membership in the interior of the dual cone. Finally $[\omega ^{n-1}]$ belongs to this interior, so every element $b$ of $\mathcal P_ A^\vee $ is a limit of $b+\varepsilon [\omega ^{n-1}]\in \mathcal B$. This proves both assertions. $\square$ Proposition 10.101.2 . 8DC16DCAD850 The balanced and movable cones satisfy \[  \overline{\mathcal B}=\mathcal M, \qquad \mathcal B=\operatorname {Int}\mathcal M.  \] Moreover, $\mathcal M$ is the closed convex cone generated by the classes $\mu _*(\kappa ^{n-1})$, where $\mu :Y\to X$ is a modification from a compact Kähler manifold and $\kappa $ is a Kähler class on $Y$. Proof. Let $j:H^{1,1}_{\mathbb R}(X)\to H_ A^{1,1}(X,\mathbb R)$ be the cohomology identification. A closed positive current is pluriharmonic, so $j(\mathcal E)\subseteq \mathcal P_ A$. For the reverse inclusion, let $T\geq 0$ be pluriharmonic and let $a=j^{-1}[T]_ A$. For a modification $\mu :Y\to X$ and Kähler forms $\omega _1,\ldots ,\omega _{n-1}$ on $Y$, choose a positive pluriharmonic current $\widetilde T$ in $\mu ^*[T]_ A$ by theorem 5.66.2 . Smooth closed test forms annihilate Aeppli boundaries, hence \[  a\cdot \mu _*[\omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{n-1}] =\int _ Y\widetilde T\wedge \omega _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{n-1} \geq 0.  \] Cone duality theorem 10.100.1 gives $a\in \mathcal E$. Thus $j(\mathcal E)=\mathcal P_ A$. Apply lemma 10.101.1 and $\mathcal E^\vee =\mathcal M$ to conclude. The single-power description is also theorem 10.100.1 . $\square$

title: 25.1 Classical potentials, boundary problems, and capacity
search_title: Classical potentials, boundary problems, and capacity
section: 25.1 Classical potentials, boundary problems, and capacity
text: Pluripotential theory grew out of the study of harmonic functions, but its development repeatedly required a change in what counts as a solution, a negligible set, or a boundary value. This chapter follows those changes through the subjects of Pome. Classical potentials lead to capacity and fine topology; plurisubharmonic functions lead to nonlinear Monge–Ampère measures; singular metrics connect these analytic constructions to complex geometry. The later sections follow this connection through equations, envelopes, energy, sections, and non-Archimedean spaces. The order follows the mathematical dependencies of the reference rather than the tables of contents of its contributing texts. The Dirichlet problem supplied one of the original organizing questions: how can boundary data determine a harmonic function inside a domain? Green functions express a solution in terms of sources, while Perron's method constructs one by taking an envelope of subsolutions. Boundary regularity then becomes a geometric question. Wiener's criterion answers it through capacity, measuring the thickness of the complement near a boundary point rather than merely its Euclidean size. The chapters on harmonic and subharmonic functions and energy, capacity, and fine topology develop these related viewpoints. Helms's account provides a classical reference for Green potentials, sweeping, boundary limits, and the Wiener test; the supplementary contributions in Pome also pursue energy and Martin boundaries. Riesz's theory of subharmonic functions made positive measures central to this picture. A subharmonic function can be studied through its distributional Laplacian and its potential representation, even where ordinary second derivatives do not exist. This explains the position of measures, distributions, and convergence near the beginning of Pome. Distributional equations, local integrability, weak convergence, and the choice of testing class are part of the analytic language needed later. Vague convergence on an open domain, for example, permits mass to escape to its boundary; convergence against all bounded continuous functions is stronger. Capacity records exceptional sets which volume alone cannot detect. Polar sets arise as pole sets of subharmonic potentials, and quasi-continuity replaces ordinary continuity by continuity outside open sets of arbitrarily small capacity. Cartan's fine topology makes superharmonic functions continuous and provides the natural setting for thinness and sweeping. Fuglede's work develops fine potential theory beyond the Euclidean framework. These ideas precede their complex analogues: the plurifine topology and nonlinear capacity inherit the same concern with exceptional sets, while using a different family of test functions. Brelot and Fuglede provide complementary classical perspectives. The classical material remains active throughout the later theory. Perron envelopes reappear in homogeneous Monge–Ampère equations and weak geodesics; capacity controls nonlinear limits; integration by parts becomes the source of energy inequalities. Pome includes Fourier analysis and complex-line incidence where these supply analytic tools, but these tools should be distinguished from the potential-theoretic structures they help establish. The historical continuity lies in the questions about positivity, envelopes, and exceptional sets. Separate harmonicity and geometric boundary tests illustrate how the classical theory interacts with several variables. Lelong and Avanissian developed the passage from separate to joint harmonicity; Avanissian's account uses harmonic expansions and complexification. Klimek also surveys the integrable-majorant theorem of Arsove and Wiegerinck's example for separate subharmonicity. The planar boundary-distance criteria are due to Armitage–Kuran and Parker. Their higher-dimensional failures require separate examples, as developed in the classical chapter ; an account of the negative-distance criterion also appears in Kuznetsov .

title: 25.2 Plurisubharmonicity, currents, and singularities
text: The passage to several complex variables begins with plurisubharmonic functions, introduced independently in the work of Oka and Lelong . Subharmonicity along complex lines provides a function-theoretic definition; positivity of the distributional complex Hessian provides its current-theoretic form. These two descriptions explain the joint treatment of plurisubharmonic functions and positive currents . Unlike real subharmonicity alone, plurisubharmonicity is adapted to holomorphic maps and complex analytic sets. Bremermann's historical account discusses the early development. Demailly's analytic exposition supplies the current-theoretic background for the homotopy formulas, complete Hartogs domains, and relative smoothing developed here. Richberg's method underlies smoothing with a variable strict-positivity bound; Klimek attributes the global decreasing smooth approximation on pseudoconvex domains to Fornæss–Narasimhan. Exceptional-set geometry has its own subtleties: Diederich–Fornæss constructed a smooth curve in complex dimension two that is not pluripolar. The construction in Pome treats every complex dimension at least two. The Green-function theory connects pseudoconvexity with invariant distances and spaces of holomorphic functions. Lempert's work establishes complex geodesics and holomorphic retractions on convex domains; stationary discs also lead to the smooth Green construction on smooth strongly convex domains. The dual extremal method is developed further by Royden–Wong–Krantz . The relation between hyperconvexity and the Fréchet space of holomorphic functions is treated by Aytuna , using the power-series-space methods of Vogt . Pome proves the bounded-domain characterization and states its hypotheses explicitly. Currents allow differential forms with singular coefficients to participate in geometric operations. The Poincaré–Lelong formula identifies the complex Hessian of a logarithm with the current of a divisor, linking zeros of holomorphic functions to positivity. Lelong numbers then quantify concentration at a point. Siu's analyticity theorem shows that suitable upper level sets of these numbers are analytic, making a numerical measure of singularity detect complex subvarieties. The notions of positivity for currents were developed by Lelong and Harvey–Knapp; they have a history distinct from later regularization techniques. Demailly's Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry develops real and complex currents alongside plurisubharmonic functions. Regularization and homotopy relate currents to smooth differential forms, while positivity provides measure coefficients and local mass bounds. Extension across complete pluripolar sets and integration over analytic sets connect this calculus to complex geometry. Slicing, generic multiplicity and Siu decomposition relate local densities to analytic cycles. The generalized Lelong–Jensen theory uses plurisubharmonic weights to measure concentration and construct boundary measures. Demailly's memoir on Monge–Ampère measures and affine algebraicity and his work on Monge–Ampère and pluriharmonic measures are central sources for this development. The admissibility of a weight and properness on the relevant current support remain part of each comparison statement. Another way to measure a singularity is to test which holomorphic germs remain square integrable against its exponential weight. Nadel's multiplier ideal sheaves turn this integrability condition into coherent algebraic data. The weighted estimates of Hörmander and the extension theorem of Ohsawa–Takegoshi supply the analytic mechanisms relating holomorphic functions to singular weights. The chapter on Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization brings these descriptions together. Our convention is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}=\mathrm i\partial\bar\partial/(2\pi)$ and the multiplier weight is $\exp(-\varphi)$; changing either convention changes numerical thresholds. The openness problem asks how stable such integrability is under a small increase in the weight. Demailly–Kollár formulated and studied the openness conjecture; Berndtsson established an openness theorem, and Guan–Zhou proved strong openness. These results are distinct from approximation statements. Bergman kernels and regularization provide controlled models of singular weights, whereas openness concerns the ideal of a fixed weight. Historical attribution to these methods does not by itself supply the hypotheses or estimates required in a particular approximation argument. The exceptional sets also have a specifically complex history. Josefson's local-to-global theorem identifies locally pluripolar sets in complex Euclidean space with global pole sets; global variants on compact manifolds require their own hypotheses. The plurifine topology is associated with Fuglede's work in the Lelong seminar. Bedford–Taylor developed its relation to nonlinear products, and El Marzguioui–Wiegerinck proved the local-connectivity result used in the theory. Keeping these contributions separate clarifies why pluripolarity, plurifine locality, and ordinary almost-everywhere identities have different roles.

title: 25.3 Nonlinear products, capacity, and mass
text: The complex Monge–Ampère operator is nonlinear: a distributional complex Hessian cannot generally be multiplied by itself. The decisive construction of Bedford–Taylor (1976) and Bedford–Taylor (1982) defines mixed products for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions by integration by parts. Continuity under monotone limits makes this definition useful beyond the smooth case. The chapter on local Monge–Ampère theory and capacity develops this calculus before the global theory uses it. The Bedford–Taylor calculus is also the starting point for the classical unbounded products treated in Demailly's exposition . Compactness or dimension conditions on the unbounded loci permit further products by controlling their mass. Such classical products can retain mass on a pole set and therefore differ from the non-pluripolar construction, which removes that mass. Weighted boundary measures and Jensen identities belong to the same classical current framework, developed in Demailly’s memoir and work on pluriharmonic measures ; their normalizations and pole terms are retained in the statements. The associated capacity measures sets by testing them against bounded plurisubharmonic potentials. It supports quasi-continuity, comparison principles, and continuity of products under suitable convergence in capacity. This convergence must be read with its domain quantifier. On an open set, monotone convergence of plurisubharmonic functions gives convergence on each compact subset; exceptional sets can escape toward the boundary with capacity bounded away from zero on the entire open set. On a compact manifold a finite covering converts the local conclusion into a global one. This distinction is the nonlinear counterpart of the escape-of-mass issue in ordinary weak convergence. Unbounded potentials require a further choice: what mass should be retained at their poles? Truncation produces bounded products, and restriction away from the truncation loci yields the non-pluripolar product. Bedford–Taylor's work on pluripolar sets, Guedj–Zeriahi , and Boucksom–Eyssidieux–Guedj–Zeriahi form successive stages of this development. The resulting measure does not charge pluripolar sets. Consequently, even in a fixed cohomology class, its total mass can decrease when the potential becomes more singular. Full mass is therefore a substantive condition. The chapter on non-pluripolar measures and mass studies the resulting order and continuity questions. Bounded changes of singularities preserve mixed masses, while comparisons between different singularity types require monotonicity theorems. Work of Witt Nyström and Darvas–Di Nezza–Lu established the mass comparisons used in the modern relative theory. These results connect local truncation arguments with global intersection numbers, and explain why assumptions about singularities must accompany statements about mass. Analytic Fujita approximation connects non-pluripolar masses with intersection theory on modifications. Boucksom's volume theory and the work of Boucksom–Demailly–Păun–Peternell develop this connection through positive currents and approximate Zariski decompositions. The movable part is represented by Kähler or nef classes upstairs, while an effective divisor records the remaining singularities. Controlling top volume and lower mixed products on the same approximating models is what makes the construction useful for variation formulas. Comparison theorems identify the maximal non-pluripolar mass with numerical approximation and with the current volume defined by the absolutely continuous determinant. The algebraic construction of positive products by Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson gives a direct approach to varying volume. A uniform quadratic lower error near a nef approximant, applied again with the endpoints exchanged, identifies the differential. This argument separates class-space variation from continuity for arbitrary weakly converging currents. Boucksom's appendix to Witt Nyström's projective duality theorem relates orthogonality, differentiability and cone duality in the analytic setting. These developments complement the non-pluripolar mass comparisons and singularity-type continuity discussed above. On a general Hermitian manifold the background form need not be closed. Bedford–Taylor products remain available locally after a smooth correction, but global integration by parts now produces torsion terms. The total mass can vary even among bounded potentials. This is the point at which the Kähler and Hermitian developments separate: the local nonlinear calculus continues to be useful, while global mass, comparison, and normalization need new estimates. The next sections follow the geometric and equation-theoretic consequences of that separation. Several local extensions explain why the domain of the operator matters. Klimek reports the obstruction of Shiffman and Taylor to a positive multilinear extension on the full plurisubharmonic cone. The regularizations attributed to Cegrell are discussed by Błocki . Generalized-function products provide another setting: Klimek credits Kiselman and Oberguggenberger, while the elementary Colombeau definitions used here are recalled by Nigsch . These constructions have different compatibility and convergence requirements. The boundary measures associated with logarithmic poles belong to the Lelong–Jensen theory developed by Demailly . Symmetry and total mass also depend on the domain geometry. Cegrell studies symmetric Green envelopes, and Bedford–Demailly give a smooth-domain asymmetry example. The smooth-boundary Fatou–Bieberbach construction of Stensønes supplies the domain used here to test total-mass comparison without properness. The comparison associated with Taylor is retained with a proper-exhaustion hypothesis; the unrestricted nonproper assertion discussed in Klimek does not survive that test.

title: 25.4 Positivity, Hermitian geometry, and volume
text: Local positive currents become global geometric objects through their cohomology classes. On a compact Kähler manifold, the $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm c}$-lemma identifies closed currents in a fixed real $(1,1)$-class with quasi-plurisubharmonic potentials, up to a constant on each connected component. This is the bridge from the local theory to cohomology, positivity, and geometric loci . Nefness, bigness, and pseudo-effectivity describe different kinds of positivity; their geometric loci record where positive representatives can or cannot be made regular. Hermitian linear algebra, Chern connections and elliptic estimates support the Hodge and vanishing theory in Demailly's book . The Frölicher spectral sequence compares Dolbeault and de Rham cohomology on general complex manifolds. Bott–Chern and Aeppli groups retain further information, while the Kähler identities impose stronger relations. The Bochner–Kodaira identity and its torsion terms distinguish the Hermitian calculation from its Kähler specialization. The $L^2$ method of Hörmander, holomorphic division and compact vanishing theorems connect curvature to global sections and jets. Kodaira’s embedding theorem and its integral-curvature formulation then relate positivity to projectivity. Unique continuation is a separate analytic ingredient: Aronszajn's theorem is a classical source for scalar-principal second-order equations and coupled lower-order inequalities. Its hypotheses do not assert unrestricted unique continuation for every matrix-principal elliptic system. Pliś's smooth elliptic counterexample provides a concrete obstruction. Its fourth-order two-variable construction can be prolonged to an ordinary second-order elliptic system with a nonzero smooth solution vanishing on an open set. This separates general matrix-principal ellipticity from the scalar-principal hypotheses used for harmonic forms. The spectral proof of holomorphic Morse inequalities uses a different asymptotic from the transcendental subtraction of nef classes. Demailly's magnetic-field method counts low Dolbeault eigenvalues and gives weak and strong line-power cohomology inequalities with a fixed coefficient bundle on compact Hermitian manifolds. Its semipositive specialization yields the leading holomorphic-section growth without assuming a Kähler base. Siu's work on semipositive line bundles over non-Kähler manifolds includes the one-point positivity variant in an added-in-proof announcement. Its geometric application joins section growth to Kähler modifications and coefficient-valued cohomological descent. The existence input for eliminating the meromorphic map is stated separately from the analytic and descent proofs. Hopf quotients illustrate the topological restrictions imposed by the Kähler condition. The normal-coordinate curvature expansion and Wirtinger’s inequality connect the local Hermitian metric to curvature and complex-volume geometry in Demailly's exposition . Boucksom's divisorial Zariski decomposition distinguishes the divisorial negative part of a pseudoeffective class from its movable positivity. Orthogonality and the derivative of volume express this structure numerically. The differentiability formula of Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson , and its transcendental extension through Witt Nyström and Boucksom , identify the gradient with the positive product of degree one less than the dimension. Cao–Tosatti establish the sharp local $C^{1,1}$ regularity once this formula is available. Their elementary cone estimate uses homogeneity and monotonicity, so the local Lipschitz bound for the gradient need not be deduced from a concavity theorem. The volume extends by zero across the non-big locus; its regularity there is a separate assertion from differentiability inside the big cone. For nef transcendental classes on compact Kähler manifolds, Tosatti's sharp Morse inequality supplies the optimal subtraction bound for volume. Its current-concentration and separation argument extends the projective numerical picture to the full real $(1,1)$-space. Together with simultaneous analytic approximation, the inequality yields volume differentiation, orthogonality, and duality of the pseudoeffective and movable cones. The separating classes may already be taken as pushforwards of single Kähler powers from modifications. The spectral holomorphic Morse inequalities discussed earlier count a different cohomological asymptotic. Restricted volumes record positivity along a specified analytic subvariety. Collins–Tosatti develop their numerical analytic formulation and its relation to non-Kähler loci. Witt Nyström's deformation to the normal bundle and Vu's work on divisorial derivatives connect these invariants with the first variation of volume. The formulation must retain the distinction between ordinary restriction outside the non-Kähler locus and the numerical extension to a subvariety in that locus. Birational reduction and the contribution of divisorial negative parts are part of that comparison. Balanced metrics provide a smooth representative for another face of the same duality. Toma establishes the relevant projective cone comparison, and Fu–Xiao develop the compact Kähler version. Their separation arguments test closed strictly positive $(n-1,n-1)$-forms against positive $\partial\bar\partial$-closed currents. The behavior of these currents under modifications is studied by Alessandrini–Bassanelli's work on balanced manifolds and their transforms of currents . Lifting these currents under a modification requires an additional theorem: $\partial\bar\partial$-closedness alone does not provide a local plurisubharmonic potential for pullback. This analytic input enters the identification of the closure of the balanced cone with the movable cone. Hermitian geometry brings a different cohomological structure. Bott–Chern and Aeppli classes retain information lost when one uses only de Rham cohomology, and their pairing is natural for positivity questions. Gauduchon metrics satisfy $\partial\bar\partial\omega^{n-1}=0$, a weaker condition than the Kähler condition $\mathrm d\omega=0$. Gauduchon's existence theorem makes this condition available within a conformal class. Lamari's positivity criterion uses dual testing against Gauduchon forms; see Lamari . These ideas organize Hermitian geometry, torsion, and Gauduchon duality . The absence of closedness changes the meaning of a volume. In the Kähler setting, Stokes' theorem fixes the mass of bounded potentials in a class. In the Hermitian setting, upper mass bounds and positive lower mass bounds are separate properties of a background. Work of Guedj–Lu and subsequent developments studies these bounds and their role in equations and singularity volumes. The distinction between a bound for each individual potential and a uniform bound over a family is essential. It is also why a theorem for a closed big class cannot be transferred verbatim to an arbitrary positive Hermitian form. The chapter on Gauduchon variational volume develops an additional variational viewpoint using Gauduchon data and duality. It should be read alongside, rather than identified with, the cohomological volume of a closed class or the mass attached to an ordinary singularity type. The historical strands meet in their use of positivity and nonlinear measures, but their admissible objects and normalizations differ. Several results in the Hermitian contribution belong to a working research exposition; original references and precise source revisions remain under Sources.

title: 25.5 Cohomology, compact curves, and complex tori
search_title: Cohomology, compact curves, and complex tori
section: 25.5 Cohomology, compact curves, and complex tori
text: Sheaf resolutions, supported products and spectral sequences organize the cohomological part of Demailly's Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry . The de Rham comparison connects this language to differential forms. Integral orientation and cap duality require local coefficient systems and retain torsion information which real differential forms do not detect. Hatcher's Algebraic Topology supplies a complementary account of the integral singular-topological theory. Compact-support duality, ordinary duality and their coefficient hypotheses are distinguished throughout these comparisons. Nuclear Fréchet tensor products and analytic direct images form a separate topological development: closed-range cohomology, actual balanced quotients and algebraic Tor groups keep their respective hypotheses. For compact complex curves the analytic and topological theories meet in Riemann–Roch, Serre duality, periods and Jacobians. Picard and Albanese tori extend the period construction, while polarizations relate integral forms to projective embeddings. These topics are presented together in Demailly's book ; their organization here follows the common cohomological and geometric structures.

title: 25.6 Monge–Ampère and complex Hessian equations
text: The complex Monge–Ampère equation links the local nonlinear operator to global geometry. Yau's solution of the Calabi conjecture in the Kähler case established the smooth theory for prescribed volume forms with the required total mass. In the weak theory, the background geometry, the regularity of the measure, and the permitted singularities of the solution become separate parts of the problem. The chapter on Monge–Ampère equations and stability follows this progression from a priori estimates to existence, uniqueness, and stability. The local Dirichlet theory of Bedford–Taylor makes the regularity of the density and the boundary geometry central to estimates. Degenerate equations require additional care: the examples after Pliś , and the regularity qualifications discussed by Dinew–Pliś–Zhang , show why smoothness of the density alone does not supply all the expected second-derivative bounds. Pome keeps these counterexamples beside the precise density-root hypotheses of the positive results. Kołodziej's bounded-solution theory for measures with $L^p$ density, $p>1$, changed the range of accessible right-hand sides. Capacity estimates replace estimates that require a smooth density and make it possible to pass to weak limits. In big classes, Boucksom–Eyssidieux–Guedj–Zeriahi constructed solutions with controlled singularities, while Berman–Boucksom–Guedj–Zeriahi developed the variational approach through energy functionals. Local energy classes originating with Cegrell provide another route from bounded functions to unbounded solutions. These approaches share nonlinear comparison tools but have different admissible classes. The Hermitian equation has a further normalization issue. Since the total mass need not be fixed by cohomology, prescribing a measure can also require determining a multiplicative constant. Cherrier's work and the smooth existence theory of Tosatti–Weinkove are basic stages of this development. The weak theory developed by Kołodziej–Nguyen and others must control the torsion errors in comparison and stability arguments. Uniqueness for a normalized solution, uniqueness of the normalization constant, and a selection principle for limits are distinct assertions; the book treats them with the corresponding assumptions. The chapter on equations with prescribed singularities asks for more than a solution in an ambient big class. Fixing an ordinary singularity type constrains how the solution may diverge, and the mass of that type must match the equation. The relative theory developed by Darvas–Di Nezza–Lu uses model potentials and relative full-mass classes to formulate this compatibility. In the Hermitian setting, the same question interacts with upper and lower mass bounds. Results for semipositive backgrounds, big closed backgrounds, and general nonclosed backgrounds therefore occupy different places in the theory. Complex Hessian equations replace the top exterior power by intermediate symmetric functions of the complex Hessian. Their admissible cones, mixed inequalities, and comparison principles extend part of the Monge–Ampère picture, but require their own ellipticity and background assumptions. Work of Dinew–Kołodziej and the Hermitian developments of Kołodziej–Nguyen are among the reference points for this subject. The parallel with Monge–Ampère theory helps organize the questions; it does not eliminate the changes in degree, positivity, or torsion.

title: 25.7 Envelopes, singularity types, and prescribed data
search_title: Envelopes, singularity types, and prescribed data
section: 25.7 Envelopes, singularity types, and prescribed data
text: An envelope is a maximal admissible potential lying below an obstacle. This construction already appears in Perron's solution of the classical Dirichlet problem. In complex geometry it also compares singularities, defines weak geodesics, and identifies where nonlinear measures can concentrate. The chapter on singularity types, envelopes, and models develops these uses together. A pointwise supremum generally needs upper semicontinuous regularization, and the discrepancy between the two is controlled by pluripolarity and capacity. Rooftop envelopes impose two upper obstacles simultaneously. Singularity envelopes instead retain an asymptotic bound on the singularity while removing inessential bounded features. The $P$-envelopes of Ross–Witt Nyström , building on ideas of Rashkovskii–Sigurdsson , helped make this language systematic. In the relative theory of Darvas–Di Nezza–Lu, model potentials provide reference singularities for full-mass and finite-energy classes. Their importance comes from the interaction between envelope contact sets and Monge–Ampère mass, rather than from a choice of normalization alone. Several distinctions are needed when using these constructions. Order up to a bounded additive term describes ordinary singularity type; literal pointwise order describes particular representatives. A rooftop envelope may be identically minus infinity unless its admissible family is nonempty. Equality of total masses does not automatically imply equality of singularity types, and a positive-mass argument may fail when the reference mass is zero. These are structural issues in the development of the theory, and explain the careful separation of envelope identities, comparison results, and zero-mass cases in Pome. Multiplier ideals give another equivalence relation. Two potentials may have the same multiplier ideals at every positive scale while differing in ordinary singularity type. The $\mathcal I$-envelope retains this integrability data. Darvas–Xia formulated the associated model theory in connection with earlier work of Dano Kim and Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson; related formulations appear in subsequent work, including Trusiani's. The chapter on multiplier-ideal models and partial equilibrium studies this additional structure. Ordinary models and multiplier-ideal models answer different questions, so neither terminology should silently replace the other. The envelope viewpoint reconnects the equation theory with algebraic approximation. A singularity constraint can be imposed analytically through an obstacle or algebraically through an ideal. The extent to which these constraints have the same mass, section growth, or energy is a theorem to be established. This is the conceptual reason that envelopes appear both before the metric theory and before the chapters on sections and non-Archimedean potentials.

title: 25.8 Energy, geodesics, rays, and metric geometry
search_title: Energy, geodesics, rays, and metric geometry
section: 25.8 Energy, geodesics, rays, and metric geometry
text: Energy measures more than the total mass of a potential: it records how the potential interacts with its own mixed Monge–Ampère measures. Cegrell's local classes and the global finite-energy theory of Guedj–Zeriahi made it possible to work with singular functions while retaining integration by parts and comparison. Relative energy uses a chosen reference singularity, allowing the same questions to be asked in a prescribed type. This is the starting point of energy, geodesics, rays, and test curves . The geometric interpretation comes from the space of Kähler metrics. Mabuchi , Semmes , and Donaldson connected its formal Riemannian geometry with a homogeneous complex Monge–Ampère equation on a product. Chen established weak geodesics for smooth endpoint data. Perron envelopes supply a pluripotential construction of these paths: boundary values become obstacles, and maximality becomes a nonlinear equation. Endpoint convergence is part of this construction and needs to be established in the topology relevant to the endpoints. Darvas's work on metric geometry and finite-energy completions gives singular potentials an intrinsic metric interpretation. The extension to big classes and relative settings was developed further by Darvas–Di Nezza–Lu and others. Completeness, geodesic existence, and energy continuity rely on the full-mass or finite-energy assumptions appropriate to the metric. A path defined by an envelope need not automatically have every metric or endpoint property of a smooth geodesic. Geodesic rays lead from paths between two potentials to asymptotic geometry. Ross–Witt Nyström's analytic test configurations relate rays and test curves through a Legendre transform. The convex parameter on the ray side becomes a singularity cutoff on the curve side. Relative energy and mass profiles then describe slopes and asymptotic invariants. This duality helps explain the appearance of convex analysis in a theory initially formulated with complex Hessians. The Hermitian contribution investigates how much of this metric picture survives when the background is not closed. The local envelope construction remains meaningful, but torsion can obstruct energy identities that in the Kähler case follow from Stokes' theorem. For this reason the book distinguishes metric completeness under its stated hypotheses from the existence of a pointwise envelope, and ordinary singularity control from multiplier-ideal control. These distinctions also matter when comparing analytic rays with the algebraic and non-Archimedean objects discussed next.

title: 25.9 Sections, convex bodies, and non-Archimedean geometry
search_title: Sections, convex bodies, and non-Archimedean geometry
section: 25.9 Sections, convex bodies, and non-Archimedean geometry
text: Singular metrics impose integrability conditions on holomorphic sections. Counting sections satisfying those conditions gives an algebraic measure of positivity, while partial Bergman kernels give an analytic measure of their distribution. The chapters on sections, graded series, and Okounkov bodies and multiplier-ideal models and partial equilibrium study how these quantities compare with nonlinear masses and envelopes. Multiplier ideals are the interface: they turn the singular weight into an ideal defining the allowed sections. Weighted Jensen formulas also lead to Schwarz-type bounds for entire functions vanishing on a finite set. Demailly's exposition relates polynomial degree, singular degree and weighted multiplicity in these inequalities. Waldschmidt's account develops the connection with transcendence and algebraic groups, including the analytic method behind Bombieri's arithmetic zero-set theorem. A coarse degree bound, the optimal asymptotic Schwarz coefficient and an exceptional-locus refinement are different assertions. Star configurations of hyperplanes realize the proposed degree bound with equality in every dimension. This special case leaves the general historical conjectures separate from the proved estimates. Okounkov's construction associates convex sets to asymptotic orders of vanishing. The volume formulas of Lazarsfeld–Mustaţă and Kaveh–Khovanskii relate Euclidean volumes of these bodies to growth of graded linear series and semigroups. Passing from an algebraic series to sections constrained by analytic singularities requires control of the relevant ideals and asymptotic growth. Pome develops the semigroup and convex arguments alongside these applications. The lattice normalization, including the factor $n!$ in the volume formula, is part of the statement. Toric geometry provides a particularly explicit bridge. The work of Atiyah, Delzant, Guillemin, Abreu, and Donaldson connects toric Kähler geometry with moment polytopes and convex functions. Pluripotential formulations were developed by Berman–Berndtsson and Coman–Guedj–Şahin–Zeriahi . In toric and convex geometry , Legendre transforms turn invariant potentials into convex data, and complex Monge–Ampère measures into real Monge–Ampère measures. This dictionary makes singularity order, rooftops, and mass calculations concrete while keeping track of their domains and boundary behavior. B-divisors and restriction organize information over different birational models. Instead of selecting one resolution permanently, a b-divisor records compatible data on models. Divisorial valuations then detect orders of singularity that a fixed coordinate chart or fixed model may miss. Restricting a singular potential is a separate operation: a trace must account for poles and for the positivity available on the subvariety. These constructions connect the analytic theory of singularities with intersection-theoretic data. Polynomial approximation gives a local and affine counterpart of these constructions. Siciak and Zaharjuta relate polynomial growth to pluripotential extremals; Siciak's product theorem and the real-body formulas of Lundin and Baran are presented in Klimek . Pleśniak's survey develops extremal functions and geometric regularity, while Kołodziej studies logarithmic capacity and Robin-function comparisons. Pome's open-semianalytic regularity proof uses real analytic principalization in the form supplied by Bierstone–Milman ; this geometric theorem remains an explicit external input. Bedford–Taylor's study of symmetric real convex bodies connects their extremal functions with explicit equilibrium densities and boundary mass. Pome develops the real Monge–Ampère calculation and the convex foliation alongside these formulas. For arbitrary rough symmetric convex bodies, the boundary-mass proof uses a projective dilation and the bounded energy cocycle; it does not infer absence of boundary mass from a limit of interior densities. This connects the affine formulas with the compact energy calculus. Non-Archimedean pluripotential theory places related information on valuation spaces and Berkovich spaces. Work of Boucksom–Favre–Jonsson , their later Monge–Ampère theory, and Boucksom–Jonsson develops positivity, envelopes, and energy in this setting. Model functions and test configurations supply algebraic approximants, while analytic rays provide an asymptotic comparison. These correspondences require precise hypotheses, including those governing mass and homogeneity; they should not be inferred merely from the repeated use of the words “potential” or “model.”

title: 25.10 Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry
search_title: Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry
section: 25.10 Singular spaces, traces, and locally conformally Kähler geometry
text: The manifold theory extends in two directions which require different tools: allowing the underlying complex space to be singular, and allowing the metric to be only locally conformal to a Kähler metric. The chapter on complex spaces and modifications supplies the analytic foundations for the first direction. The chapter on Hopf and locally conformally Kähler geometry develops the second through concrete geometric models. Their common use of local potentials should not obscure their different global obstructions. On a complex space, plurisubharmonicity can be tested through local embeddings and holomorphic discs. The theorem of Fornæss–Narasimhan is a central reference for the disc characterization. Extension and proper-image results make it possible to compare intrinsic functions with ambient analytic data. Resolutions and principalization then replace singular spaces or ideals by smooth models with controlled divisors. Pome treats Hironaka's resolution and principalization as external geometric inputs; the analytic estimates used after passing to a resolution remain separate arguments. The local geometry of analytic sets, normalization and modifications also provides a common setting for extension and coherent-sheaf methods. Demailly's book joins these geometric constructions to Cartan's cohomology theorems, proper direct images and convexity estimates. Nilpotent structure requires the full quotient structure sheaf; the underlying zero set alone does not determine a complex space. Affine algebraicity also involves growth at infinity, whereas local analytic parametrization concerns a neighborhood of one point. Bounded strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions on smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domains are the subject of Diederich–Fornæss . Their exponent and boundary hypotheses accompany the exhaustion estimate. This work is distinct from the later smooth nonpluripolar-curve example. Passing to a smooth model still leaves the analytic extension and descent arguments to establish. Projective models and Kähler modifications connect meromorphic maps to compact geometry. Demailly's author-hosted Analytic Methods in Algebraic Geometry is the specified reference for resolving a bimeromorphic map from a compact Kähler manifold by smooth-center blowups of its source. This elimination existence theorem remains an explicit external input; reconstructing the surrounding analytic and cohomological descent arguments does not provide a proof of elimination. Unibranchness and related local hypotheses affect how potentials and measures behave across singularities. A result valid on a resolution does not automatically descend to every singular space, and a restriction to a subvariety may be identically minus infinity. The trace constructions in b-divisors and restriction address this problem by specifying how singularity data is transferred. These questions explain the continued interaction between modifications, multiplier ideals, and non-pluripolar products. A locally conformally Kähler metric has a closed Lee form and becomes Kähler after a local conformal change. On a suitable covering space, deck transformations act by homotheties, so global potentials may carry an automorphy condition. Hopf manifolds offer concrete examples where this geometry can be studied without assuming a global Kähler form. The work of Ornea–Verbitsky and the related literature on Vaisman and locally conformally Kähler manifolds provides the geometric background for the final geometric chapter. The Perron constructions used there impose both positivity and the relevant equivariance or boundary condition. Descending a function from the cover, selecting a normalization, and solving the local nonlinear equation are distinct steps. These examples bring the book back to the classical envelope method, but in a setting where topology and conformal geometry change the admissible potentials. They also show why the common organization of Pome follows mathematical subjects rather than treating each source manuscript as a separate theory.

title: 25.11 Perspectives and further reading
text: The preceding history follows three recurring transitions: from functions to measures and currents, from bounded potentials to controlled singularities, and from local constructions to global geometric data. Each transition introduces a new compatibility question. Products need a domain of definition; capacities need a testing region; equations need a mass normalization and a singularity class; algebraic comparisons need a precise correspondence between ideals, valuations, and analytic potentials. These questions account for the organization of the reference and for many of its open problems. A reader approaching the subject through analysis can follow harmonic and subharmonic functions through capacity and the bounded Bedford–Taylor operator, then proceed to non-pluripolar measures and weak equations. A geometric route begins with positive currents, multiplier ideals, and cohomological positivity, then moves to singularity envelopes and section growth. Energy and geodesics connect the two routes, while toric examples give explicit convex models. The Hermitian and locally conformally Kähler chapters examine which parts of these constructions persist when closedness or a global potential is unavailable. For classical potential theory, Brelot and Helms provide complementary accounts of harmonic spaces and Euclidean potentials. For pluripotential theory, Klimek and Guedj–Zeriahi provide broad treatments; Demailly's analytic texts explain the current-theoretic and weighted analytic background. The papers cited in the preceding sections supply more specific starting points for non-pluripolar products, variational equations, relative singularities, metric geometry, and algebraic asymptotics. The bibliography collects these references, and Sources retains the original bibliographical notes and exact contributing revisions. Klimek's 1991 monograph is a principal reference for affine extremals, capacities, local Green functions, and invariant distances. Demailly's homotopy and smoothing methods provide shared analytic tools. Cegrell's monograph on capacities gives another account of the local theory and its envelope constructions. These texts offer complementary routes through the subjects developed in the preceding historical sections. The chapter on problems in pluripotential theory contains the formally stated conjectures and questions, including those formerly placed among historical comments. They retain their own permanent tags. Historical attribution identifies the origin and development of an idea; it neither replaces a proof nor asserts priority for the additional arguments in this reference. Where a contribution is a working research draft, the statement, its assumptions, and its recorded source should be consulted together.
